     2	Reading the Law
     3	Text in small capitals defines key terms. 
     4	Text in italics gives reminders and clarifi­
     5	cations. Faction icons mark rules modified 
     6	by Faction Rules and Abilities sections.
     7	Root contains two rulebooks: the Learning to Play guide 
     8	and this book, the Law. If you like a conversational 
     9	teaching style and many graphical examples, read the 
    10	Learning to Play guide. If you like a strictly defined, 
    11	formal rules in a concise reference style, read the Law.
    12	These rules of thumb will help you interpret the Law.
    13	Q1. I’d like to do something, and the rules don’t say 
    14	that I can’t do it. Can I do it?
    15	A1. Within the confines of the action, yes! The game will often 
    16	surprise you with outlandish, unexpected situations, and that’s 
    17	part of the fun, but this doesn’t mean you can flip the table.
    18	Q2. It seems like something should happen, but the 
    19	rule doesn’t tell me to do that thing. What do I do?
    20	A2. Follow the literal word of the Law, not your instinct, even 
    21	if a similar rule exists. 
    22	Q3. A rule uses a specific term or action. Does it also 
    23	include another, closely related term or action?
    24	A3. Nope! Assume we mean only the original term and not 
    25	any related terms. For example, the terms move and place 
    26	are different. For specific term definitions, see the Glossary 
    27	(Appendix G). 
    28	If you have any other questions, check our website for 
    29	more answers: ledergames.com/root
    30	If you have any missing or damaged components, you 
    31	can go here for support: ledergames.com/replacements
    32	If you have questions about specific cards, go to the 
    33	Leder Card Library: cards.ledergames.com
    34	1. Golden Rules
    35	This chapter gives answers to technical, detailed ques­
    36	tions. You do not need to read it when first learning.
    37	1.1 Rules Conflicts
    38	1.1.1     Precedence. If a card conflicts with the Law, fol­
    39	low the card. If the Learning to Play guide con­
    40	flicts with the Law, follow the Law. If you can fol­
    41	low both a general rule and a faction or hireling 
    42	rule, follow both; if you cannot, follow the faction 
    43	or hireling rule.
    44	1.1.2     Use of Cannot. The term cannot is absolute. It 
    45	cannot be overridden unless explicitly instructed.
    46	1.1.3     Unclear Resolutions and Choices. Whenever it 
    47	is unclear what order simultaneous effects should 
    48	resolve in, or which player should make a deci­
    49	sion, the player taking their turn chooses.
    50	1.2 Public and Private Information
    51	1.2.1     Hands. Players may only show or reveal cards in 
    52	their hand if explicitly instructed, but the number 
    53	of cards in their hand is public information. O
    54	1.2.2     Piles and the Shared Deck. Face-up piles such 
    55	as the discard pile can be searched and inspected. 
    56	The shared deck cannot.
    57	1.3 Negotiation, Deals, and Consent
    58	1.3.1     Agreements. Players may discuss the game and 
    59	make agreements, but they are non-binding.
    60	1.3.2     Cards. Players may only give cards to each other 
    61	if explicitly instructed.
    62	1.3.3     Consent. Actions never require consent.
    63	1.4 Game Structure
    64	1.4.1     Turn Structure. Each player’s turn has three 
    65	phases: Birdsong, Daylight, and Evening. Any­
    66	thing that says “at start of” a phase happens be­
    67	fore everything else in the phase, and anything 
    68	that says “at end of” happens after everything else 
    69	in the phase but before the start of the next phase, 
    70	if any. After a player ends Evening, the next clock­
    71	wise player begins their turn. Play continues until 
    72	one player has won the game (3.1).
    73	1.4.2     Interrupts. You cannot interrupt an action (in­
    74	cluding a compound action such as the Marquise’s 
    75	March), ability (such as the Corvids’ Exposure), or 
    76	persistent effect (such as the Eyrie Emigre card) with 
    77	another effect unless it explicitly allows it. (For ex­
    78	ample, the Armorers card says it is used “In battle...”).
    79	1.4.3     End of Turn. Once a player begins the last step of 
    80	their turn, they cannot take actions except those 
    81	that specify “end of Evening” or “end of turn,” 
    82	such as hirelings (Appendix H).
    83	1.5 Pieces
    84	1.5.1     Limits. Pieces are limited by the contents of the 
    85	game. Do not use proxy pieces if you run out.
    86	1.5.2     Starting Faction. Each player owns the faction 
    87	they choose in setup (5) and the pieces listed on 
    88	the back of its faction board except for items. Ge­
    89	nerically, these are called faction pieces or sim­
    90	ilar. Specifically, these are called [faction name] 
    91	pieces. (For example, “your faction warriors” and 
    92	“warriors of your faction” and “Marquise warriors” all 
    93	refer to the orange wooden cat-shaped warriors.)  
    94	1.5.3     Piece Ownership. The ownership of faction piec­
    95	es cannot change. (For example, the Marquise can­
    96	not use Field Hospitals on Riverfolk mercenaries or 
    97	hirelings, since these are not Marquise warriors.)
    98	1.5.4     Piece Manipulation. Pieces are placed and re­
    99	moved as defined in the Glossary (G.20, G.24). If 
   100	you are prompted to place, take, or remove pieces
